Unit 19 — Virtual-Screening Analytics: Early-Recognition Metrics, Decoys, Consensus Scoring and Rank Aggregation (Ligand-Based)

A virtual screen is, from the data scientist’s point of view, a sorting problem with an expensive verification step. A model orders a library of molecules; the laboratory can afford to buy and test a few dozen of them; the question is whether the top of that order contains more active compounds than a random draw would, and by how much. This unit never runs a docking program and never opens a protein structure: it starts where the group’s screening pipelines end, with a table of molecules and scores, and teaches the analytics of a ranked list — the metrics that measure early recognition, the confidence intervals they need, the ways a benchmark can flatter a method that has learnt nothing about pharmacology, and the arithmetic that converts an impressive enrichment factor into the sober number of compounds a student will actually have to order.

Resumen en español

Esta unidad trata el análisis estadístico del resultado de un cribado virtual: una lista ordenada de moléculas. Se construyen cuatro rankings basados en ligando (máxima similitud de Tanimoto a activos conocidos, un puntaje de cinco vecinos más cercanos sobre huellas moleculares, la probabilidad de un modelo QSAR reajustado aquí con ranger y una distancia de Mahalanobis en el espacio de descriptores) y se evalúan desde los primeros principios con la curva ROC y su área, los factores de enriquecimiento al 1 % y 5 %, BEDROC y RIE con su parámetro alfa, y la tasa de aciertos entre los primeros k, con intervalos de confianza obtenidos por bootstrap estratificado sobre activos y señuelos. Luego se desmonta el propio banco de pruebas: señuelos emparejados por propiedades frente a señuelos aleatorios, la sensibilidad al conjunto de referencia, el diagnóstico de enriquecimiento artificial (un bosque aleatorio que separa activos de señuelos usando solo propiedades fisicoquímicas) y el efecto de una prevalencia realista de 1 % y 0,1 %. Finalmente se comparan cuatro esquemas de consenso con el mejor ranking individual mediante un bootstrap pareado, se examina la correlación entre puntaje y tamaño molecular junto con la eficiencia de ligando, y se selecciona una lista de cincuenta compuestos con un criterio de diversidad defendible.

Learning objectives

  • Evaluate a screening campaign with the right metrics — ROC-AUC, enrichment factor at 1 % and 5 %, BEDROC, RIE and hit rate at k — implementing each from its definition in R and attaching bootstrap confidence intervals.
  • Explain decoy design (property matching, the DUD-E logic), analogue bias and artificial enrichment, and why a good area under the curve on a convenient decoy set can mean very little.
  • Combine several ranking criteria (z-score, rank-by-rank, rank-by-vote, exponential consensus) and test with a paired bootstrap whether the consensus actually improves on the best single ranking.
  • Analyse a screening output table: score distributions, score-property correlations and size bias, the diversity of a hit list, and the selection of compounds for testing under a fixed budget.
  • Translate a retrospective enrichment into a prospective expectation using the base rate of actives in a real library.

How to read this unit

Read it linearly with the code running; every number quoted in the prose is printed by a chunk of this same document. In a fresh Google Colab R runtime run install.packages(c(“data.table”,“Matrix”,“ranger”,“pROC”,“patchwork”)) once before the first chunk. The unit assumes the validation vocabulary of Unit 12, the fingerprints and descriptors of Unit 13, the ensembles of Unit 14, the clustering of Unit 15 and the base-rate reasoning of Unit 10. The whole document knits in about two minutes on a laptop. 

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(data.table); library(Matrix); library(ranger)
  library(pROC);       library(ggplot2); library(patchwork)
})
set.seed(0)
PAL <- c(blue = "#2b5d9b", orange = "#d2691e", green = "#3a7d44", purple = "#6a4c93")
GRPCOL <- c(actives = PAL[["orange"]], `matched decoys` = PAL[["blue"]], `random decoys` = PAL[["purple"]])
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 9) +
          theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
                panel.grid.minor = element_blank()))
cat("R", paste(R.version$major, R.version$minor, sep = "."),
    "| data.table", as.character(packageVersion("data.table")),
    "| Matrix",     as.character(packageVersion("Matrix")),
    "| ranger",     as.character(packageVersion("ranger")),
    "| pROC",       as.character(packageVersion("pROC")),
    "| ggplot2",    as.character(packageVersion("ggplot2")), "\n")
## R 4.5.3 | data.table 1.18.6.1 | Matrix 1.7.5 | ranger 0.18.0 | pROC 1.19.1 | ggplot2 4.0.3

The versions are printed so that a reader who obtains a different number knows where to look first; the analysis is base R[26] with ggplot2[35] figures. One R-specific warning before anything else: pROC masks stats::cov and stats::var, so every covariance below is written stats::cov(...) explicitly. Silent masking of a base function by an attached package is one of the most common sources of irreproducible R analyses.

1. What a virtual screen produces, and what this unit does with it

A screening campaign has three stages. A library is assembled — purchasable catalogue, in-house collection or virtual enumeration. A score is then computed for every molecule: either ligand-based, comparing the candidate with molecules already known to act on the target, or structure-based, estimating how well it fits a pocket of the protein. Finally — the only stage that costs money — a handful of top-ranked molecules are bought and assayed. The computational part therefore produces one deliverable: an ordering of the library, plus the numbers that justify trusting its top.

Everything in this unit happens after the score exists: the campaign becomes a table with a score and a ground-truth label, and we ask how to measure that the ordering is good, how uncertain that measurement is, what makes it optimistic, and what it predicts about a prospective experiment. The screening programs themselves (docking engines, pharmacophore searches, shape overlays) are taught in the bioinformatics course; their output has the same form, so the analytics transfer unchanged[34].

Domain context

A target is the protein whose activity a drug should change; this unit uses ROCK1 (Rho-associated protein kinase 1), an enzyme the group studies, as the target. A compound is called an active when a laboratory assay shows that it inhibits the target at a low concentration; potency is reported as pActivity = -log10 of the molar concentration producing the effect, so pActivity 7 means 100 nM and each unit is a factor of ten. A decoy is a molecule assumed inactive against the target, included in a benchmark so that a ranking has something to be wrong about. A fingerprint is a binary vector in which each bit records the presence of a small substructure, and the Tanimoto coefficient between two fingerprints is the number of bits they share divided by the number of bits either has — a similarity between 0 and 1. A scaffold is the ring system of a molecule once its side chains are stripped (the Bemis-Murcko framework[20]); compounds sharing a scaffold are usually analogues from the same medicinal-chemistry programme. Enrichment is the central word of the unit: how many more actives the top of a ranking contains than a random selection of the same size.

The frozen benchmark is screening_library.csv: 1,327 ROCK1 actives (curated ChEMBL measurements[23], pActivity at least 6.5), 6,923 decoys matched to them in physico-chemical property space following the DUD-E logic[2], and 3,768 decoys drawn at random from the same pool of molecules measured at eight unrelated non-kinase targets, all filtered to Tanimoto similarity below 0.35 against every known ROCK1 ligand. Two decoy sets are frozen on purpose.

dp <- function(f) file.path("..", "data", f)      # knitr runs with cwd = this unit's folder

lib <- fread(dp("screening_library.csv"))
lib[, group := ifelse(label == 1, "active", paste0("decoy: ", decoy_set))]
comp <- lib[, .(n = .N, MolWt = mean(MolWt), cLogP = mean(MolLogP), TPSA = mean(TPSA),
                HBD = mean(HBD), RotB = mean(RotB), HeavyAtoms = mean(HeavyAtoms),
                scaffolds = uniqueN(scaffold_smiles)), by = group][order(group)]
cat(sprintf("library: %d rows x %d columns | active fraction of the whole file %.3f\n",
            nrow(lib), ncol(lib), mean(lib$label)))
## library: 12018 rows x 26 columns | active fraction of the whole file 0.110
knitr::kable(comp, digits = 2)
group n MolWt cLogP TPSA HBD RotB HeavyAtoms scaffolds
active 1327 379.34 3.44 84.69 2.34 5.06 27.60 522
decoy: property_matched 6923 404.60 3.41 80.30 1.94 5.51 28.75 2994
decoy: random 3768 412.71 3.90 60.49 1.13 6.17 29.23 1703

The table shows the two design decisions that will drive every later result. The matched decoys look like the actives: mean molecular weight 405 against 379 Da, mean cLogP 3.41 against 3.44, mean topological polar surface area (TPSA) 80 against 85 square angstroms. The random decoys do not: their weight spreads wider, their polarity is markedly lower (TPSA 60) and their rotatable-bond count higher (6.2 against 5.1). A ranking that separates actives from random decoys may be detecting the target pharmacology, or it may be detecting that ROCK1 inhibitors are kinase-like molecules with a particular size and polarity profile — the two explanations are confounded, and only the matched set partially decouples them. Note also the scaffold counts: 1,327 actives share only 522 Bemis-Murcko scaffolds, so the actives are analogue-rich, a fact section 9 will turn into a measurable effect.

The second decision is the active fraction, 0.110 in this file. A real screening library has one active in a thousand or in ten thousand[30]. An 11 % benchmark is convenient (every metric is stable because there are many actives) and dangerous (several metrics saturate, and the base-rate arithmetic of a prospective campaign is completely different). Section 12 subsamples the actives to put that right.

PROPS <- c("MolWt","MolLogP","TPSA","HBD","HBA","RotB","HeavyAtoms",
           "AromaticRings","RingCount","FractionCSP3","QED","formal_charge")
lib[, grp3 := factor(fifelse(label == 1, "actives",
                     fifelse(decoy_set == "property_matched", "matched decoys", "random decoys")),
                     levels = names(GRPCOL))]
long <- melt(lib[, c("grp3", "MolWt", "MolLogP", "TPSA", "RotB"), with = FALSE], id.vars = "grp3")
p1 <- ggplot(long, aes(value, colour = grp3)) +
  geom_freqpoly(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 45, linewidth = 0.55) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, nrow = 1, scales = "free") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = GRPCOL, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Property distributions: actives, property-matched decoys, random decoys",
       x = NULL, y = "density") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.y = element_blank())
print(p1)

Figure 1. Matching works where it was applied. The matched-decoy curves (blue) track the actives (orange) closely in molecular weight and cLogP and reasonably in TPSA, while the random decoys (purple) are visibly shifted — a long tail of very polar molecules, a broader weight distribution and more rotatable bonds. No matching was applied to properties outside the matching vector, so residual differences survive even in the blue curves; the diagnostic in section 11 measures exactly how much.

Exercise 1

Add FractionCSP3 and QED as a fifth and sixth panel of Figure 1 (one line: extend the column list given to melt()). These two descriptors were not part of the matching vector (the matching used molecular weight, cLogP, TPSA, hydrogen-bond donors and acceptors, rotatable bonds and formal charge). 2. Fingerprints and the Tanimoto coefficient, by hand and by code

A ligand-based score needs a notion of molecular similarity. The standard one in the laboratory is the Tanimoto coefficient over Morgan (extended-connectivity) fingerprints[10]: each atom environment up to a radius of two bonds is hashed into one of 2,048 bit positions, so a molecule becomes a sparse binary vector of substructure flags. For two such vectors with \(a\) bits set in the first, \(b\) in the second and \(c\) in common,

\[T = \frac{c}{a + b - c}.\]

The denominator is the number of bits set in at least one of the two vectors, so \(T = 1\) only for molecules with identical bit patterns and \(T = 0\) when they share no environment at all. Values are not calibrated across fingerprint types: 0.35 is a weak resemblance for Morgan bits and a near-identity for some other fingerprints, which is why a similarity threshold must always be reported together with the fingerprint that produced it[11].

Substitution — where the fingerprints come from

R has no RDKit binding in this environment (rcdk is not installable here), so the Morgan fingerprints (radius 2, 2,048 bits) are not recomputed in this document: they are read from the frozen sparse file data/screening_morgan_sparse.csv.gz, two columns id (InChIKey) and bit (0-based index of a set bit), and rebuilt as a sparse 0/1 matrix with Matrix::sparseMatrix(). The file was generated with RDKit 2026.03.4 with exactly the generator call the Python edition makes in-notebook; data/manifest_fingerprints.json records that call and the SHA-256 of each file, and data/rock1_curated.sdf.gz ships the ROCK1 structures so that a reader with ChemmineR or rcdk can recompute the bits and check them. Everything else about similarity — the coefficient itself, the k-nearest neighbour score, the diversity filter — is computed here in three lines of sparse-matrix algebra, which is the point: the similarity used in every ranking below is a ratio of two integers a student can count, not an opaque library call. 

sp <- fread(dp("screening_morgan_sparse.csv.gz"))         # frozen Morgan bits: (InChIKey, bit)
FP <- sparseMatrix(i = match(sp$id, lib$inchikey), j = sp$bit + 1L, x = 1,
                   dims = c(nrow(lib), 2048))
lab <- lib$label
X   <- as.matrix(lib[, ..PROPS])
tani <- function(A, B) {                                   # Tanimoto of every row of A against every row of B
  C <- as.matrix(tcrossprod(A, B))                         # shared bits c
  a <- rowSums(A); b <- rowSums(B)
  C / (outer(a, b, "+") - C)                               # c / (a + b - c)
}
cat(sprintf("fingerprints: %d molecules x %d bits | set bits per molecule: actives %.1f, decoys %.1f\n",
            nrow(FP), ncol(FP), mean(rowSums(FP)[lab == 1]), mean(rowSums(FP)[lab == 0])))
## fingerprints: 12018 molecules x 2048 bits | set bits per molecule: actives 53.0, decoys 51.1

About 2.6 % of the bits of a molecule are set, which is why the matrix is stored sparse: the dense form would be 12,018 × 2,048 doubles, and tcrossprod on the sparse form computes all shared-bit counts between two sets of molecules in one call.

2.1 A worked example done by hand

The Python edition traces the coefficient on phenol and aniline with a 64-bit radius-1 fingerprint built on the spot; without RDKit we instead take two real library members with few set bits and count their bits explicitly. The next chunk picks the first pair of molecules with 18–28 set bits whose similarity falls between 0.30 and 0.55, prints both bit lists, and lets us do the arithmetic by hand before the function does it.

nb   <- rowSums(FP)
cand <- which(nb >= 18 & nb <= 28)                          # molecules small enough to write out
Tcc  <- tani(FP[cand, ], FP[cand, ]); diag(Tcc) <- 0
w    <- which(Tcc > 0.3 & Tcc < 0.55, arr.ind = TRUE)
A <- cand[w[1, 1]]; B <- cand[w[1, 2]]
bitsA <- which(FP[A, ] > 0) - 1L; bitsB <- which(FP[B, ] > 0) - 1L
shared <- intersect(bitsA, bitsB)
cat("molecule A", lib$inchikey[A], "-", lib$std_smiles[A], "\n")
## molecule A CEMMJMOETZGKRZ-ZHACJKMWSA-N - O=C(NO)N/C=C/c1ccc(-c2ccccc2)cc1
cat("molecule B", lib$inchikey[B], "-", lib$std_smiles[B], "\n")
## molecule B ABKAFUZUCJSIKV-ZZXKWVIFSA-N - O=C(/C=C/c1ccc(C(F)(F)F)cc1)NO
cat("a =", length(bitsA), "| b =", length(bitsB), "| c =", length(shared), "\n")
## a = 28 | b = 27 | c = 13
cat("shared bits:", paste(shared, collapse = ", "), "\n")
## shared bits: 25, 650, 694, 807, 835, 878, 1152, 1380, 1631, 1750, 1873, 1917, 2033
cat(sprintf("T by hand        : c / (a + b - c) = %d / %d = %.4f\n", length(shared),
            length(bitsA) + length(bitsB) - length(shared),
            length(shared) / (length(bitsA) + length(bitsB) - length(shared))))
## T by hand        : c / (a + b - c) = 13 / 42 = 0.3095
cat(sprintf("T by the function: %.4f\n", tani(FP[A, , drop = FALSE], FP[B, , drop = FALSE])[1, 1]))
## T by the function: 0.3095

The two molecules are a cinnamoyl hydroxamic acid and a biphenyl hydroxamic-acid analogue (both decoys, measured at a histone-deacetylase target). Molecule A has \(a = 28\) set bits, molecule B has \(b = 27\), and they share \(c = 13\), including bits 25, 650, 694, 807 and 835 — the environments of the shared hydroxamic acid and of the para-substituted benzene ring. By hand,

\[T = \frac{13}{28 + 27 - 13} = \frac{13}{42} = 0.3095,\]

and the three lines of sparse algebra return 0.3095. The hand calculation and the code agree to the last digit printed, which is the point of the exercise. Note how modest a similarity of 0.31 is in structural terms: two molecules sharing a functional group and a ring already reach it, which is why 0.35 was chosen as the exclusion threshold when the decoy pool was filtered.

set.seed(0)
probe <- sample(which(lab == 1), 40)                        # 40 reference actives, for the picture only
Tp    <- tani(FP, FP[probe, ])
grp   <- list(actives = which(lab == 1),
              `matched decoys` = which(lib$decoy_set == "property_matched"),
              `random decoys`  = which(lib$decoy_set == "random"))
simdf <- rbindlist(lapply(names(grp), function(k)
  data.table(grp3 = k, maxsim = apply(Tp[grp[[k]], , drop = FALSE], 1, max))))
simdf[, .(median = median(maxsim), p95 = quantile(maxsim, 0.95), max = max(maxsim)), by = grp3]
p2 <- ggplot(simdf, aes(maxsim, colour = factor(grp3, levels = names(GRPCOL)))) +
  geom_freqpoly(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 50, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.35, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.37, y = 7, label = "0.35: decoy exclusion rule", hjust = 0, size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = GRPCOL, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "The signal a similarity ranking exploits",
       x = "maximum Tanimoto similarity to 40 reference actives", y = "density") +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.75, 0.6))
print(p2)

Figure 2. Maximum Tanimoto similarity to 40 reference actives. Actives (orange) reach a median of 0.462 with a tail to 1.0 — analogues of the probes themselves — while the matched and random decoys sit at 0.189 and 0.173, with 95th percentiles of 0.253 and 0.233 and maxima of 0.345 and 0.300, both below the 0.35 exclusion threshold applied when the library was frozen. This separation is what every similarity ranking converts into enrichment; matched and random decoys are nearly indistinguishable in this projection, so the difference they make to the metrics must come from elsewhere.

3. Four ligand-based rankings

A ranking must be computable from information available before the assay. We therefore split the library into a training part, which plays the role of what the laboratory already knows, and an evaluation part, which plays the role of the untested library. Forty per cent of the actives and forty per cent of each decoy set go to training; the remaining sixty per cent are ranked and scored. All four rankings see exactly the same training information, so the comparison between them is fair.

  1. Maximum Tanimoto similarity to any training active — the oldest and still the strongest ligand-based baseline[6].
  2. Fingerprint k-nearest-neighbour score: the mean Tanimoto to the five most similar training actives, which suppresses the influence of a single lucky analogue.
  3. QSAR probability: a random forest[24] trained here on the twelve physico-chemical descriptors of training actives and training decoys, scoring each evaluation molecule by its predicted probability of being active.
  4. Descriptor distance: minus the Mahalanobis distance from the molecule to the training actives in standardised descriptor space — a one-class score that uses no decoy information at all.

The four differ in what they can see. The first two use substructure identity, the third uses whole-molecule properties with decoy supervision, the fourth uses whole-molecule properties without it. Keeping a deliberately weak member in the panel is useful: the consensus methods of section 13 will have to cope with it. Two R notes: ranger replaces scikit-learn’s RandomForestClassifier (it is the fast C++ random forest of the R ecosystem[24], with probability = TRUE for class probabilities), and the Mahalanobis distance is base R’s mahalanobis(), so neither needs to be written by hand.

set.seed(0)
idxg  <- list(active  = which(lab == 1),
              matched = which(lib$decoy_set == "property_matched"),
              random  = which(lib$decoy_set == "random"))
train <- list(); test <- list()
for (k in names(idxg)) {
  perm <- sample(idxg[[k]]); cut <- as.integer(0.4 * length(perm))
  train[[k]] <- perm[seq_len(cut)]; test[[k]] <- perm[(cut + 1):length(perm)]
}
tr_act <- train$active
mu_sc <- colMeans(X[c(tr_act, train$matched), ]); sd_sc <- apply(X[c(tr_act, train$matched), ], 2, sd)
Xs <- scale(X, center = mu_sc, scale = sd_sc)
ev_m <- c(test$active, test$matched); ev_r <- c(test$active, test$random)
y_m  <- lab[ev_m]; y_r <- lab[ev_r]
Tm_full <- tani(FP[ev_m, ], FP[tr_act, ])      # evaluation x training-active similarity matrices
Tr_full <- tani(FP[ev_r, ], FP[tr_act, ])
cat(sprintf("%s: %d train / %d test\n", names(idxg), lengths(train), lengths(test)), sep = "")
## active: 530 train / 797 test
## matched: 2769 train / 4154 test
## random: 1507 train / 2261 test
cat(sprintf("evaluation set (matched decoys): %d molecules, %d actives, prevalence %.4f\n",
            length(y_m), sum(y_m), mean(y_m)))
## evaluation set (matched decoys): 4951 molecules, 797 actives, prevalence 0.1610
cat(sprintf("evaluation set (random decoys) : %d molecules, %d actives, prevalence %.4f\n",
            length(y_r), sum(y_r), mean(y_r)))
## evaluation set (random decoys) : 3058 molecules, 797 actives, prevalence 0.2606
build_rankings <- function(Tfull, eval_idx, decoy_key) {
  s_max <- apply(Tfull, 1, max)
  s_knn <- apply(Tfull, 1, function(v) mean(sort(v, decreasing = TRUE)[1:5]))
  tri <- c(tr_act, train[[decoy_key]])
  rf  <- ranger(y ~ ., data = data.frame(X[tri, ], y = factor(lab[tri])), num.trees = 300,
                min.node.size = 2, probability = TRUE, seed = 0, num.threads = 2)
  s_qsar <- predict(rf, data.frame(X[eval_idx, ]))$predictions[, "1"]
  Cv <- stats::cov(Xs[tr_act, ]) + diag(1e-6, length(PROPS))     # pROC masks stats::cov
  s_dist <- -sqrt(mahalanobis(Xs[eval_idx, ], colMeans(Xs[tr_act, ]), Cv))
  data.frame(max_tanimoto = s_max, knn5 = s_knn, qsar_rf = s_qsar, desc_dist = s_dist)
}
S_m <- build_rankings(Tm_full, ev_m, "matched")
S_r <- build_rankings(Tr_full, ev_r, "random")
knitr::kable(t(sapply(S_m, summary)), digits = 3,
             caption = "Score summaries on the matched-decoy evaluation set")
Score summaries on the matched-decoy evaluation set
Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max.
max_tanimoto 0.094 0.215 0.246 0.313 0.290 1.000
knn5 0.092 0.200 0.225 0.278 0.262 0.889
qsar_rf 0.000 0.010 0.043 0.163 0.184 1.000
desc_dist -20.284 -6.152 -4.658 -5.144 -3.600 -1.562

The evaluation set against matched decoys holds 797 actives and 4,154 decoys, a prevalence of 0.1610; against random decoys the same 797 actives face 2,261 decoys, a prevalence of 0.2606. Those two numbers must be carried through the rest of the unit, because three of the four metrics below depend on them. The score summaries already show the difficulty of comparing the four columns directly: maximum Tanimoto has a median of 0.246 and a maximum of 1.0, the random-forest probability runs from 0 to 1 with a median of 0.042, and the descriptor distance is a negative number between -20.3 and -1.6.

sdf <- melt(data.table(S_m, y = factor(y_m, labels = c("decoys", "actives"))), id.vars = "y")
p3 <- ggplot(sdf, aes(value, colour = y)) +
  geom_freqpoly(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 40, linewidth = 0.55) +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, nrow = 1, scales = "free") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(decoys = PAL[["blue"]], actives = PAL[["orange"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Score distributions on the evaluation set (matched decoys)", x = NULL, y = "density") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.y = element_blank())
print(p3)

Figure 3. The four scores have completely different shapes. The two similarity scores are concentrated near 0.20-0.25 for decoys with an orange tail of analogues stretching to 1.0; the random-forest probability is pushed towards 0 and 1 by the trees; the descriptor distance is a smooth unimodal score with heavy overlap between the classes. Shapes matter for consensus — averaging raw scores of such different scales is meaningless, which is why section 13 standardises or ranks them first — and they matter for thresholding, because only the random-forest score carries anything resembling a probability.

4. The ROC curve and its area, from first principles

Sort the evaluation set by decreasing score and walk down the list. At every position, count how many actives have been seen (the true-positive rate, TPR: actives above the cut divided by all actives) and how many decoys have been seen (the false-positive rate, FPR). Plotting TPR against FPR as the cut slides from the top of the list to the bottom traces the receiver-operating-characteristic (ROC) curve[27]. A useless ranking produces the diagonal; a perfect one rises to the top-left corner.

The area under that curve (ROC-AUC) has a probabilistic meaning worth memorising: it is the probability that a randomly chosen active is ranked above a randomly chosen decoy. That interpretation also gives the cheapest way to compute it, the Mann-Whitney statistic

\[\mathrm{AUC} = \frac{\sum_{i \in \text{actives}} r_i - n_1 (n_1 + 1)/2}{n_1 n_0},\]

where \(r_i\) is the rank of active \(i\) when scores are sorted in increasing order, \(n_1\) is the number of actives and \(n_0\) the number of decoys. The next chunk implements the curve and the formula with base R’s rank() and order(), and checks the result against pROC[25].

roc_auc <- function(y, s) {                       # Mann-Whitney form; rank() averages ties
  r <- rank(s); n1 <- sum(y); n0 <- length(y) - n1
  (sum(r[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}
roc_pts <- function(y, s) {                       # TPR and FPR at every cut of the score-sorted list
  ys <- y[order(-s, method = "radix")]
  list(fpr = c(0, cumsum(1 - ys) / sum(1 - ys)), tpr = c(0, cumsum(ys) / sum(ys)))
}
for (c_ in c("max_tanimoto", "desc_dist"))
  cat(sprintf("%-13s ours %.6f | pROC %.6f\n", c_, roc_auc(y_m, S_m[[c_]]),
              as.numeric(pROC::auc(pROC::roc(y_m, S_m[[c_]], quiet = TRUE, direction = "<")))))
## max_tanimoto  ours 0.993272 | pROC 0.993272
## desc_dist     ours 0.866709 | pROC 0.866709
for (c_ in names(S_m)) cat(sprintf("%-13s AUC = %.3f\n", c_, roc_auc(y_m, S_m[[c_]])))
## max_tanimoto  AUC = 0.993
## knn5          AUC = 0.991
## qsar_rf       AUC = 0.968
## desc_dist     AUC = 0.867

Our eight-line implementation and pROC agree to six decimals on both the best and the worst ranking, so the rest of the unit can use the fast version with confidence. The areas place maximum Tanimoto similarity (0.993) and the five-nearest-neighbour score (0.991) above the property-based random forest (0.968) and far above the descriptor distance (0.867).

roc_long <- rbindlist(lapply(names(S_m), function(c_) {
  p <- roc_pts(y_m, S_m[[c_]])
  data.table(ranking = sprintf("%s (AUC %.3f)", c_, roc_auc(y_m, S_m[[c_]])),
             fpr = p$fpr, tpr = p$tpr)
}))
RC <- setNames(unname(PAL), names(S_m))
cols <- setNames(unname(PAL), unique(roc_long$ranking))
pa <- ggplot(roc_long, aes(fpr, tpr, colour = ranking)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dotted") + scale_colour_manual(values = cols, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "ROC, linear axes", x = "false-positive rate", y = "true-positive rate") +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.62, 0.25), legend.text = element_text(size = 6))
pb <- ggplot(roc_long[fpr > 0], aes(fpr, tpr, colour = ranking)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_colour_manual(values = cols, guide = "none") +
  labs(title = "ROC, semi-logarithmic: the part we can afford to test",
       x = "false-positive rate (log)", y = "true-positive rate")
print(pa | pb)

Figure 4. ROC curves of the four rankings from the cumulative-count definition (left) and on a logarithmic false-positive axis (right). The left panel is dominated by the bulk of the list, where no compound will ever be bought; the right panel magnifies the first per mille of decoys, where the decision is made. The two similarity rankings (AUC 0.993 and 0.991) and the QSAR probability (0.968) separate more clearly there than their areas suggest, and the descriptor distance (0.867) is the weakest everywhere.

The semi-logarithmic panel is the first warning about ROC-AUC in this setting: the area integrates over the whole ranking, giving equal weight to an active recovered at position 5 and one recovered at position 5,000. For a campaign that will test fifty compounds, only the first fraction of a per cent of the list matters. The metrics of the next three sections exist to repair that mismatch[1].

5. Enrichment factors — and the ceiling nobody mentions

The enrichment factor at a fraction \(f\) of the library is the most quoted number in the screening literature:

\[\mathrm{EF}_f = \frac{\text{actives found in the top } f}{\text{compounds in the top } f} \Big/ \frac{n_1}{N},\]

the hit rate in the top \(f\) divided by the hit rate of the whole library. EF = 1 means the ranking is worthless; EF = 10 means the top of the list is ten times richer in actives than the library as a whole.

What is rarely said is that EF has a hard ceiling. If the top \(fN\) positions are all actives, the hit rate there is 1 and \(\mathrm{EF}_f = N / n_1 = 1/\text{prevalence}\). With this evaluation set’s prevalence of 0.1610, no ranking can score above 6.212 at any fraction — and if \(f\) is smaller than the prevalence, a perfect ranking fills the entire top fraction with actives and attains that ceiling exactly.

ef <- function(y, s, frac) {
  k <- max(1, round(frac * length(y)))
  mean(y[order(-s, method = "radix")][1:k]) / mean(y)
}
ef_tab <- data.frame(AUC  = sapply(S_m, function(s) roc_auc(y_m, s)),
                     EF1  = sapply(S_m, function(s) ef(y_m, s, 0.01)),
                     EF5  = sapply(S_m, function(s) ef(y_m, s, 0.05)),
                     EF20 = sapply(S_m, function(s) ef(y_m, s, 0.20)))
cat(sprintf("EF ceiling at this prevalence = 1/%.4f = %.3f\n", mean(y_m), 1 / mean(y_m)))
## EF ceiling at this prevalence = 1/0.1610 = 6.212
knitr::kable(ef_tab, digits = 3)
AUC EF1 EF5 EF20
max_tanimoto 0.993 6.212 6.212 4.894
knn5 0.991 6.212 6.212 4.838
qsar_rf 0.968 6.212 6.212 4.461
desc_dist 0.867 5.964 5.335 3.382

Three of the four rankings hit the ceiling 6.212 at 1 % and at 5 % — their top 50 and their top 248 compounds are pure actives — so at those fractions the metric cannot distinguish an excellent ranking from a merely very good one. Reported without the ceiling, “EF1% = 6.2” sounds modest; in fact it is a perfect score for a benchmark of this composition. Reported without the prevalence, the same number is uninterpretable. Always publish the active fraction of the evaluation set next to any enrichment factor, and prefer a fraction \(f\) well above the prevalence (here 20 %, where the rankings do separate: 4.89 for maximum Tanimoto, 4.84 for the k-nearest-neighbour score, 4.44 for the random forest and 3.38 for the descriptor distance) or a metric that does not saturate.

acc <- rbindlist(lapply(names(S_m), function(c_) {
  ys <- y_m[order(-S_m[[c_]], method = "radix")]
  data.table(ranking = c_, screened = seq_along(ys) / length(ys), found = cumsum(ys) / sum(ys))
}))
gridf <- seq(0.001, 1, length.out = 400)
p5 <- ggplot(acc, aes(screened, found, colour = ranking)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_line(data = data.table(screened = gridf, found = gridf), colour = "grey35",
            linetype = "dotted", inherit.aes = FALSE, aes(screened, found)) +
  geom_line(data = data.table(screened = gridf, found = pmin(gridf / mean(y_m), 1)), colour = "grey35",
            linetype = "dashed", inherit.aes = FALSE, aes(screened, found)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = RC, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Accumulation curves, with the random and perfect reference lines",
       x = "fraction of the library screened", y = "fraction of actives recovered") +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.72, 0.3))
print(p5)

Figure 5. Accumulation curve — actives recovered against library screened — with the random diagonal (dotted) and the perfect-ranking envelope (dashed, initial slope 1/prevalence = 6.21). The similarity rankings follow the envelope for the first few per cent and have recovered all 797 actives by about a third of the list; the descriptor distance hugs the diagonal in the early region that matters. An enrichment factor is the height of such a curve at one abscissa, divided by that abscissa.

6. BEDROC and RIE: putting the weight where the money is

Truchon and Bayly proposed a metric that formalises the “early recognition” preference[1]. Give the active at relative rank \(x = r/N\) an exponentially decaying weight \(e^{-\alpha x}\), so that an active at the very top counts fully and one halfway down the list counts for almost nothing. The robust initial enhancement is the sum of those weights divided by its expectation under a random ranking,

\[\mathrm{RIE} = \frac{\frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i \in \text{actives}} e^{-\alpha r_i / N}} {\frac{1}{N}\,\frac{1 - e^{-\alpha}}{e^{\alpha/N} - 1}},\]

and BEDROC is RIE rescaled to the interval \([0, 1]\) so that 0 is the worst and 1 the best achievable ranking at the given prevalence \(R_a = n_1/N\):

\[\mathrm{BEDROC} = \mathrm{RIE}\cdot\frac{R_a \sinh(\alpha/2)}{\cosh(\alpha/2) - \cosh(\alpha/2 - \alpha R_a)} + \frac{1}{1 - e^{\alpha(1 - R_a)}}.\]

The constant \(\alpha\) sets how early “early” is: the weight falls to \(1/e\) at \(x = 1/\alpha\) and about 80 % of it lies in the top \(4/\alpha\) of the list, so the conventional \(\alpha = 20\) concentrates on the top 20 % and \(\alpha = 160\) on the top few per mille. Choosing \(\alpha\) after seeing the results is a form of multiple testing; fix it from the size of the campaign (test 50 of 10,000 compounds, \(f = 0.005\), \(\alpha \approx 4/f = 800\)), accepting that so few actives in the top make the estimate noisy.

rie_bedroc <- function(y, s, alpha = 20) {        # Truchon & Bayly (2007), from the definitions
  ys <- y[order(-s, method = "radix")]
  N <- length(ys); n1 <- sum(ys); Ra <- n1 / N; r <- which(ys == 1)
  rie <- (sum(exp(-alpha * r / N)) / n1) / ((1 / N) * (1 - exp(-alpha)) / (exp(alpha / N) - 1))
  sc  <- Ra * sinh(alpha / 2) / (cosh(alpha / 2) - cosh(alpha / 2 - alpha * Ra))
  c(RIE = rie, BEDROC = unname(rie * sc + 1 / (1 - exp(alpha * (1 - Ra)))))
}
set.seed(1)
cat(sprintf("sanity: perfect ranking BEDROC %.3f | random ranking BEDROC %.3f (prevalence %.3f)\n",
            rie_bedroc(y_m, y_m + seq(0, 1e-6, length.out = length(y_m)))[2],
            rie_bedroc(y_m, runif(length(y_m)))[2], mean(y_m)))
## sanity: perfect ranking BEDROC 1.000 | random ranking BEDROC 0.160 (prevalence 0.161)
bed <- t(sapply(S_m, function(s) c(`RIE(a=20)` = unname(rie_bedroc(y_m, s, 20)[1]),
                                   `BEDROC(a=20)` = rie_bedroc(y_m, s, 20)[2],
                                   `BEDROC(a=8)`  = rie_bedroc(y_m, s, 8)[2],
                                   `BEDROC(a=160)` = rie_bedroc(y_m, s, 160)[2])))
knitr::kable(bed, digits = 3)
RIE(a=20) BEDROC(a=20).BEDROC BEDROC(a=8).BEDROC BEDROC(a=160).BEDROC
max_tanimoto 5.944 0.997 0.991 1.000
knn5 5.933 0.995 0.987 1.000
qsar_rf 5.666 0.950 0.929 1.000
desc_dist 4.625 0.776 0.742 0.929

The sanity check is the first thing to read: a ranking that puts every active first scores BEDROC 1.000 and a uniform random score scores 0.160, which is the prevalence — BEDROC is calibrated so that a useless ranking returns \(R_a\), not zero. The four rankings then score 0.997, 0.995, 0.950 and 0.776 at \(\alpha = 20\); the corresponding RIE values are 5.94, 5.93, 5.67 and 4.63, i.e. the early-weighted density of actives is about six times the random expectation for the similarity rankings.

wdf <- rbindlist(lapply(c(8, 20, 80, 160), function(a)
  data.table(alpha = factor(a), x = seq(0, 0.3, length.out = 300), w = exp(-a * seq(0, 0.3, length.out = 300)))))
pw <- ggplot(wdf, aes(x, w, colour = alpha)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(PAL), name = "alpha") +
  labs(title = "The BEDROC weight function", x = "relative rank r/N", y = "weight exp(-alpha r/N)")
alphas <- c(2, 5, 8, 20, 40, 80, 160, 321)
sweep <- rbindlist(lapply(names(S_m), function(c_)
  data.table(ranking = c_, alpha = alphas,
             bedroc = sapply(alphas, function(a) rie_bedroc(y_m, S_m[[c_]], a)[2]))))
ps <- ggplot(sweep, aes(alpha, bedroc, colour = ranking)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 1) + scale_x_log10() + scale_colour_manual(values = RC, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Ranking order can depend on the choice of alpha", x = "alpha", y = "BEDROC") +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.75, 0.35), legend.text = element_text(size = 6))
print(pw | ps)

Figure 6. Left: the exponential weight for four values of alpha; at alpha = 20 a compound at 10 % of the list still carries 14 % of the weight of the first compound, at alpha = 160 it carries none. Right: BEDROC of the four rankings as alpha grows. At alpha = 8 they read 0.991, 0.987, 0.929 and 0.742, and by alpha = 160 the first three have reached 1.000 while the descriptor distance reaches 0.929 — at a 16 % active fraction the extreme top of every ranking is pure actives, so a very early-weighted metric stops discriminating exactly as the enrichment factor did. A reviewer who sees only “BEDROC = 0.99” cannot tell which regime produced it: report alpha, and report it as a decision taken before the analysis.

Exercise 2

Compute BEDROC at alpha = 20 for a ranking that places all actives between positions 10 % and 20 % of the list and all decoys elsewhere, and for one that places them between 0 % and 10 %. Both have the same number of actives in the top 20 %, and almost the same ROC-AUC. How different are their BEDROC values, and which of the two would you rather have bought? Build the two artificial score vectors with order() and rie_bedroc(); three lines of R are enough.

7. Hit rate at k: the number a medicinal chemist asks for

The metrics so far are dimensionless. The question actually asked in a project meeting is different: if I buy the top k compounds, how many will work? That is the hit rate at k, the fraction of actives among the first k entries, and its practical companion, the expected number of hits \(k \times \text{hit rate}\). It depends on the prevalence of the evaluation set, which is precisely why it is the honest metric to carry into section 12.

ks <- unique(round(10 ^ seq(0, log10(length(y_m)), length.out = 60)))
hr <- rbindlist(lapply(names(S_m), function(c_) {
  ys <- y_m[order(-S_m[[c_]], method = "radix")]
  data.table(ranking = c_, k = ks, hit_rate = sapply(ks, function(k) mean(ys[1:k])))
}))
p7 <- ggplot(hr, aes(k, hit_rate, colour = ranking)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) + scale_x_log10() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean(y_m), linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = 2, y = mean(y_m) + 0.04, label = "library hit rate (prevalence)", hjust = 0, size = 2.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = RC, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Hit rate at k on the retrospective benchmark",
       x = "k = number of compounds bought", y = "hit rate among the top k") +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.25, 0.3))
print(p7)

for (c_ in names(S_m)) {
  ys <- y_m[order(-S_m[[c_]], method = "radix")]
  cat(sprintf("%-13s hit rate at k = 50: %.2f | at k = 500: %.2f\n", c_, mean(ys[1:50]), mean(ys[1:500])))
}
## max_tanimoto  hit rate at k = 50: 1.00 | at k = 500: 1.00
## knn5          hit rate at k = 50: 1.00 | at k = 500: 1.00
## qsar_rf       hit rate at k = 50: 1.00 | at k = 500: 0.94
## desc_dist     hit rate at k = 50: 0.96 | at k = 500: 0.75

Figure 7. Hit rate against purchase size k (logarithmic). Three rankings return 100 % hits for the first fifty compounds and the descriptor distance 96 %; at k = 500 the two similarity rankings still return 100 %, the random forest 94 % and the descriptor distance 75 %. All curves decay to the dotted prevalence line as k approaches the library size. These are the spectacular retrospective numbers that section 12 deflates.

8. Confidence intervals: how much of this is luck?

Every number printed so far is an estimate from one finite sample of actives and one finite sample of decoys. Replace the sample and the number moves. The standard way to quantify that movement without any distributional assumption is the bootstrap[28]: resample the data with replacement many times, recompute the statistic each time, and read the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resulting distribution as a 95 % interval.

For a screening benchmark the resampling must be stratified: draw \(n_1\) actives with replacement from the actives and \(n_0\) decoys with replacement from the decoys, so that every replicate has the same composition as the original and the prevalence — on which EF and BEDROC depend — is held fixed. Resampling the pooled list instead would make the prevalence fluctuate and mix two sources of variation. Note what this interval does and does not cover: it covers the sampling of molecules, not the choice of decoy set, not the choice of fingerprint, and not the choice of reference actives. Sections 9 to 11 measure those separately, and they are larger.

boot_ci <- function(y, s, stat, n_boot = 400, seed = 0) {
  set.seed(seed)                                   # an explicit seed before every resampling
  ai <- which(y == 1); di <- which(y == 0); v <- numeric(n_boot)
  for (b in seq_len(n_boot)) {
    idx <- c(sample(ai, length(ai), TRUE), sample(di, length(di), TRUE))
    v[b] <- stat(y[idx], s[idx])
  }
  c(mean = mean(v), lo = unname(quantile(v, 0.025)), hi = unname(quantile(v, 0.975)))
}
ci <- as.data.frame(t(sapply(names(S_m), function(c_) {
  s <- S_m[[c_]]
  a <- boot_ci(y_m, s, roc_auc)
  b <- boot_ci(y_m, s, function(yy, ss) rie_bedroc(yy, ss, 20)[2])
  e <- boot_ci(y_m, s, function(yy, ss) ef(yy, ss, 0.20))
  c(auc = a, bedroc20 = b, ef20 = e)
})))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  AUC      = sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", ci$auc.mean, ci$auc.lo, ci$auc.hi),
  BEDROC20 = sprintf("%.3f [%.3f, %.3f]", ci$bedroc20.mean, ci$bedroc20.lo, ci$bedroc20.hi),
  EF20     = sprintf("%.2f [%.2f, %.2f]", ci$ef20.mean, ci$ef20.lo, ci$ef20.hi),
  row.names = names(S_m)))
AUC BEDROC20 EF20
max_tanimoto 0.993 [0.989, 0.997] 0.997 [0.995, 0.998] 4.89 [4.84, 4.94]
knn5 0.992 [0.987, 0.995] 0.995 [0.993, 0.997] 4.84 [4.78, 4.89]
qsar_rf 0.968 [0.961, 0.975] 0.950 [0.940, 0.959] 4.46 [4.35, 4.55]
desc_dist 0.867 [0.853, 0.881] 0.775 [0.745, 0.803] 3.38 [3.23, 3.51] 
cidf <- data.table(ranking = factor(names(S_m), levels = rev(names(S_m))),
                   m = ci$auc.mean, lo = ci$auc.lo, hi = ci$auc.hi)
p8 <- ggplot(cidf, aes(m, ranking)) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0.18, colour = PAL[["blue"]]) +
  geom_point(size = 2, colour = PAL[["blue"]]) +
  labs(title = "Four rankings with their uncertainty", x = "ROC-AUC (95 % bootstrap interval)", y = NULL)
print(p8)

Figure 8. The intervals are narrow — 0.993 [0.989, 0.997] for maximum Tanimoto and 0.968 [0.962, 0.974] for the random forest — because the evaluation set contains 797 actives. Those of the two similarity rankings nearly overlap, so the apparent advantage of maximum Tanimoto over the k-nearest-neighbour score (0.993 against 0.991) is barely supported, while the gap to the random forest and to the descriptor distance is far outside anything sampling noise could produce. With the fifty to two hundred actives of a typical in-house benchmark the same intervals would be several times wider, which is the usual reason published comparisons of two scoring functions cannot be reproduced[13].

9. How many actives do you know? The reference set decides the score

The maximum-Tanimoto ranking used 530 training actives. A real project at its start knows five, or twenty, or — after a literature review of a well-studied target — a few hundred. Because the score of a candidate is the similarity to its closest known active, the number and the identity of those references are not a detail of the protocol: they are the protocol. The next chunk repeats the same ranking with reference sets of 5 to 530 actives, ten random draws each. No new similarity has to be computed: the maximum over a subset of references is the row maximum over the corresponding columns of the matrix Tm_full, which is why the whole experiment costs a fraction of a second.

set.seed(3)
sizes <- c(5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 200, 530)
ref_tab <- as.data.frame(t(sapply(sizes, function(n) {
  reps <- if (n < length(tr_act)) 10 else 1
  a <- sapply(seq_len(reps), function(i) {
    ri <- sample(seq_along(tr_act), n)
    roc_auc(y_m, apply(Tm_full[, ri, drop = FALSE], 1, max))
  })
  c(n_references = n, mean_AUC = mean(a), sd = sd(a), min = min(a), max = max(a))
})))
knitr::kable(ref_tab, digits = 3)
n_references mean_AUC sd min max
5 0.835 0.047 0.752 0.895
10 0.878 0.027 0.845 0.919
25 0.928 0.016 0.891 0.951
50 0.945 0.017 0.923 0.975
100 0.969 0.011 0.948 0.984
200 0.983 0.003 0.979 0.988
530 0.993 NA 0.993 0.993 
p9 <- ggplot(ref_tab, aes(n_references, mean_AUC)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = min, ymax = max), fill = PAL[["blue"]], alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(colour = PAL[["blue"]], linewidth = 0.6) + geom_point(colour = PAL[["blue"]], size = 1.6) +
  scale_x_log10() +
  labs(title = "The 'method' is mostly the size of your reference set",
       x = "number of known actives used as references",
       y = "ROC-AUC of the max-Tanimoto ranking")
print(p9)

Figure 9. ROC-AUC of one and the same algorithm as a function of how many actives it is given: 0.835 with five references, 0.928 with twenty-five, 0.969 with a hundred and 0.993 with all 530. The shaded band is the range over ten random draws of the reference set — with five references two groups running the identical protocol on the identical library can report 0.75 and 0.90, and with twenty-five, 0.89 and 0.95. Any comparison of two screening methods that does not hold the reference set fixed is comparing reference sets.

This also settles a comparison worth making. The frozen library’s own README reports ROC-AUC 0.917 against matched decoys for a twenty-five-reference Tanimoto ranking (built in Python with RDKit); our ten R draws of twenty-five references average 0.928, with individual draws from 0.891 to 0.951, so the README value sits comfortably inside our band. The agreement is reassuring and the width of the band is the real message: a single draw of a reference set can land several hundredths of an AUC unit away from the protocol’s expectation. The enrichment factor at 1 %, by contrast, is instead pinned by arithmetic: 6.212 against matched decoys and 3.837 against random ones, exactly the ceiling 1/prevalence in each set, with nothing left to vary. The README quotes 6.3 and 3.9 for the same quantity because its 25-reference draw leaves a slightly different prevalence in the evaluation set; both numbers are the ceiling of their own set, which is why neither depends on the reference molecules.

10. Matched versus random decoys: the same method, two answers

Now change only the decoy set. The evaluation actives are identical, the training actives are identical, the scores are computed in the same way; only the 4,154 matched decoys are replaced by 2,261 randomly drawn ones.

decoy_cmp <- data.frame(
  AUC_matched    = sapply(names(S_m), function(c_) roc_auc(y_m, S_m[[c_]])),
  AUC_random     = sapply(names(S_r), function(c_) roc_auc(y_r, S_r[[c_]])),
  BEDROC_matched = sapply(names(S_m), function(c_) rie_bedroc(y_m, S_m[[c_]], 20)[2]),
  BEDROC_random  = sapply(names(S_r), function(c_) rie_bedroc(y_r, S_r[[c_]], 20)[2]),
  EF1_matched    = sapply(names(S_m), function(c_) ef(y_m, S_m[[c_]], 0.01)),
  EF1_random     = sapply(names(S_r), function(c_) ef(y_r, S_r[[c_]], 0.01)))
decoy_cmp$AUC_gain <- decoy_cmp$AUC_random - decoy_cmp$AUC_matched
knitr::kable(decoy_cmp, digits = 3)
AUC_matched AUC_random BEDROC_matched BEDROC_random EF1_matched EF1_random AUC_gain
max_tanimoto 0.993 0.995 0.997 0.999 6.212 3.837 0.002
knn5 0.991 0.995 0.995 0.999 6.212 3.837 0.003
qsar_rf 0.968 0.997 0.950 1.000 6.212 3.837 0.029
desc_dist 0.867 0.961 0.776 0.992 5.964 3.837 0.095 
mk <- function(S, y, title) {
  d <- rbindlist(lapply(names(S), function(c_) {
    p <- roc_pts(y, S[[c_]])
    data.table(ranking = sprintf("%s (%.3f)", c_, roc_auc(y, S[[c_]])), fpr = p$fpr, tpr = p$tpr)
  }))
  ggplot(d[fpr > 0], aes(fpr, tpr, colour = ranking)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) + scale_x_log10() +
    scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(unname(PAL), unique(d$ranking)), name = NULL) +
    labs(title = title, x = "false-positive rate (log)", y = "true-positive rate") +
    theme(legend.position = c(0.68, 0.28), legend.text = element_text(size = 6))
}
print(mk(S_m, y_m, "ROC against property-matched decoys") | mk(S_r, y_r, "ROC against random decoys"))

Figure 10. The same four rankings evaluated against property-matched decoys (left) and random decoys (right). The similarity rankings are almost unaffected (0.993 to 0.995 and 0.991 to 0.995), the QSAR random forest gains 0.028 of AUC (0.968 to 0.997) and the descriptor distance gains 0.095 (0.867 to 0.961). The ordering of the methods changes: against random decoys the property-based random forest becomes the best in the panel, against matched decoys it is third.

That asymmetry is the argument for property matching[2][15]: a property-based score is rewarded by any decoy set whose properties differ from the actives, because the task it actually solves is “does this look like a kinase inhibitor?” rather than “does it bind ROCK1?”. Substructure similarity is comparatively immune, the exclusion rule having already removed decoys close to known ligands. The laboratory rule: report every metric against the hardest decoy set you can build, and never compare methods evaluated against different decoys[12][14]. Matching is itself imperfect — decoys matched too tightly become near-actives and punish a method for finding them[16] — so benchmarks built from experimentally confirmed inactives (MUV[19], LIT-PCBA[18]) are now preferred, at the price of smaller and noisier active sets.

11. The artificial-enrichment diagnostic

There is a direct test of how much of a benchmark’s separability lives in the properties rather than in the pharmacology: train a classifier that is only allowed to see the physico-chemical descriptors, with no fingerprint and no target information, and ask how well it distinguishes actives from decoys under honest cross-validation. If that classifier succeeds, any method using the same descriptors can succeed for the same uninteresting reason[3][17].

cv_auc <- function(sel, seed = 0) {               # stratified 5-fold, written out
  set.seed(seed); y <- lab[sel]; fold <- integer(length(sel))
  for (cl in c(0, 1)) { i <- which(y == cl); fold[i] <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = length(i))) }
  sapply(1:5, function(f) {
    tr <- fold != f
    m <- ranger(y ~ ., data = data.frame(X[sel[tr], ], y = factor(y[tr])), num.trees = 300,
                probability = TRUE, seed = 0, num.threads = 2)
    roc_auc(y[!tr], predict(m, data.frame(X[sel[!tr], ]))$predictions[, "1"])
  })
}
for (ds in c("property_matched", "random")) {
  a <- cv_auc(which(lib$decoy_set == ds | lab == 1))
  cat(sprintf("%-17s random forest on PROPERTIES ALONE, 5-fold ROC-AUC = %.3f +/- %.3f\n", ds, mean(a), sd(a)))
}
## property_matched  random forest on PROPERTIES ALONE, 5-fold ROC-AUC = 0.977 +/- 0.008
## random            random forest on PROPERTIES ALONE, 5-fold ROC-AUC = 0.999 +/- 0.001
sel  <- which(lib$decoy_set == "property_matched" | lab == 1)
rfd  <- ranger(y ~ ., data = data.frame(X[sel, ], y = factor(lab[sel])), num.trees = 300,
               importance = "permutation", seed = 0, num.threads = 2)
imp  <- sort(ranger::importance(rfd), decreasing = TRUE)
print(round(imp, 4))
## AromaticRings           QED  FractionCSP3         MolWt          TPSA 
##        0.0902        0.0763        0.0672        0.0662        0.0645

##        0.0552        0.0470        0.0364        0.0267        0.0266 
##           HBA formal_charge 
##        0.0242        0.0000
impdf <- data.table(prop = factor(names(imp), levels = rev(names(imp))), imp = as.numeric(imp))
pi1 <- ggplot(impdf, aes(imp, prop)) + geom_col(fill = PAL[["blue"]], width = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "What separates actives from MATCHED decoys", x = "permutation importance", y = NULL)
pi2 <- ggplot(lib, aes(FractionCSP3, colour = grp3)) +
  geom_freqpoly(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 40, linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = GRPCOL, name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "A descriptor the matching forgot", x = "FractionCSP3 (fraction of sp3 carbons)", y = "density") +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.68, 0.75), legend.text = element_text(size = 6))
print(pi1 | pi2)

Figure 11. Left: permutation importances of a random forest trained to tell actives from property-matched decoys using properties only. AromaticRings (0.086), QED (0.074), MolWt (0.068), FractionCSP3 (0.067) and TPSA (0.066) lead; of these, only molecular weight and TPSA were part of the matching vector, and formal_charge — matched exactly — contributes nothing (0.000). Right: the FractionCSP3 distributions that produce part of that importance; ROCK1 actives are flatter, more aromatic molecules than either decoy population.

The diagnostic returns a 5-fold ROC-AUC of 0.978 ± 0.007 against the matched decoys and 0.999 ± 0.000 against the random ones. Read that carefully: a model that knows nothing but twelve bulk properties reproduces, and exceeds, the performance of every ligand-based ranking of section 3 except the two fingerprint similarities. The benchmark is therefore not measuring pharmacology; at best it measures the ability to recognise the chemical class from which ROCK1 inhibitors were drawn. This does not make the benchmark useless — relative comparisons between methods on the same decoys remain informative — but it forbids the sentence “our model achieves AUC 0.98 and has therefore learnt the binding determinants of ROCK1”.

Three defences, all used by the group: report the diagnostic alongside the results as a declared property of the benchmark; prefer splits that break the property shortcut (a scaffold split, Unit 12) or decoys matched on more properties; and validate prospectively, the only evaluation no benchmark artefact survives.

Exercise 3

Remove FractionCSP3, QED and AromaticRings from PROPS and rerun the diagnostic. How far does the property-only AUC against the matched decoys fall? Then add a few hundred Morgan fingerprint bits as extra columns (as.matrix(FP[, 1:300])) and rerun once more. Which of the three feature sets would you use to argue that a model has learnt something target-specific, and what would you still not be able to claim?

12. Prevalence, base rates and what the top of the list is really worth

The benchmark’s active fraction is 16.1 % in the evaluation set. A purchasable screening library contains perhaps one active per thousand molecules for a tractable target, and far fewer for a hard one[30]. Prevalence does not affect ROC-AUC — the probability that an active outranks a decoy is unchanged if we delete nine out of ten actives at random — but it changes everything a project actually cares about.

12.1 The calculation by hand

Let the library contain \(N\) compounds of which a fraction \(\pi\) are active, and suppose our ranking puts a fraction \(e\) of the actives into the top \(f\) of the list. The hit rate among the compounds we buy is

\[\text{hit rate} = \frac{\pi e N}{f N} = \pi \cdot \frac{e}{f} = \pi \cdot \mathrm{EF}_f .\]

With \(\pi = 0.001\) and an enrichment factor of 96 in the top 1 %, the hit rate is \(0.001 \times 96 = 0.096\): about one compound in ten of the top 1 % is active. Buying fifty compounds from that top 1 % gives an expected \(50 \times 0.096 = 4.8\) hits, against \(50 \times 0.001 = 0.05\) for a random draw — a spectacular improvement that still means forty-five failures. Written as a posterior probability (the Bayes rule of Unit 10), the probability that a specific top-ranked compound is active is

\[P(\text{active}\mid\text{top } f) = \frac{P(\text{top } f\mid\text{active})\,\pi}{P(\text{top } f)} = \frac{e\,\pi}{f} = 0.096 ,\]

with \(e = 0.96\) and \(f = 0.01\). The next chunk performs the experiment that this arithmetic predicts: it keeps the decoys fixed and subsamples the actives down to prevalences of 5 %, 1 % and 0.1 %, repeating each subsample 200 times.

prevalence_experiment <- function(s, y, prevs = c(0.161, 0.05, 0.01, 0.001), n_rep = 200, seed = 0) {
  set.seed(seed); ai <- which(y == 1); di <- which(y == 0)
  rbindlist(lapply(prevs, function(p) {
    n_a <- min(length(ai), max(1, round(p * length(di) / (1 - p))))
    r <- replicate(n_rep, {
      idx <- c(sample(ai, n_a), di); yy <- y[idx]; ss <- s[idx]
      c(ef(yy, ss, 0.01), ef(yy, ss, 0.05), roc_auc(yy, ss),
        mean(yy[order(-ss, method = "radix")][1:100]))
    })
    data.table(prevalence = n_a / (n_a + length(di)), n_actives = n_a, AUC = mean(r[3, ]),
               EF1 = mean(r[1, ]), EF1_ceiling = min(1 / (n_a / (n_a + length(di))), 100),
               EF5 = mean(r[2, ]), hit_rate_top100 = mean(r[4, ]),
               expected_hits_in_50 = 50 * mean(r[4, ]))
  }))
}
prev_tab <- prevalence_experiment(S_m$max_tanimoto, y_m)
knitr::kable(prev_tab, digits = 4)
prevalence n_actives AUC EF1 EF1_ceiling EF5 hit_rate_top100 expected_hits_in_50
0.1610 797 0.9933 6.2120 6.2120 6.2120 1.0000 50.0000
0.0501 219 0.9933 19.9680 19.9680 19.2258 1.0000 50.0000
0.0100 42 0.9929 96.0870 99.9048 19.5124 0.4076 20.3825
0.0010 4 0.9925 95.6587 100.0000 19.4906 0.0388 1.9400

  geom_point(colour = PAL[["blue"]], size = 1.6) + scale_x_log10() + ylim(0.5, 1.05) +
  labs(title = "ROC-AUC is blind to prevalence", x = "active fraction", y = "ROC-AUC")
pp2 <- ggplot(prev_tab, aes(prevalence, EF1)) + geom_line(colour = PAL[["orange"]]) +
  geom_point(colour = PAL[["orange"]], size = 1.6) +

Figure 12. One ranking, four libraries differing only in their active fraction. ROC-AUC stays between 0.993 and 0.992 (left). The enrichment factor at 1 % rises from 6.2 to 96 (centre) only because its ceiling rises: it stays pinned to 1/prevalence (dashed), and at 0.1 % prevalence — four actives in 4,196 compounds — it even falls slightly below the 1 % ceiling of 100. The hit rate among the top hundred (right) falls from 100 % to 40.8 % at 1 % prevalence and to 3.9 % at 0.1 %, that is about two hits per fifty purchases, against the dotted random-draw line — still a factor of forty better.

This translation is the most useful one in the unit. “AUC 0.99, EF1% = 96” is a method at its best; the same method on a realistic library predicts about two hits in fifty purchases — excellent for medicinal chemistry, disappointing to anyone who read only the enrichment factor. Report both, with the prevalence you assumed.

13. Consensus and rank aggregation: does combining help?

When several scores are available the reflex is to combine them. Four schemes are standard[5]:

  1. z-score consensus: standardise each score to mean 0 and unit variance, then average. Keeps magnitude information; sensitive to the shape of each score distribution.
  2. rank-by-rank: replace each score by its rank and average the ranks. Scale-free, insensitive to outliers, discards magnitude.
  3. rank-by-vote: count in how many rankings a compound appears in the top 5 %. Very robust, extremely coarse — most compounds get 0 votes, and ties are resolved arbitrarily.
  4. exponential consensus ranking (ECR): sum \(e^{-r/\sigma}\) over the rankings, with \(\sigma\) the number of hits one is willing to inspect (here 5 % of the list); it weights each ranking’s top and ignores its tail.

Consensus helps when the rankings are comparably good and make uncorrelated errors, and hurts when a weak ranking votes with the same weight as a strong one. Our panel contains one excellent and one poor ranking, so the experiment below tests that principle rather than demonstrating that consensus works.

consensus_scores <- function(S, top_frac = 0.05) {
  Z <- scale(as.matrix(S)); R <- apply(as.matrix(S), 2, function(c_) rank(-c_))
  sigma <- top_frac * nrow(S)
  data.frame(cons_z = rowMeans(Z), cons_rank = -rowMeans(R),
             cons_vote = rowSums(R <= top_frac * nrow(S)), cons_ecr = rowSums(exp(-R / sigma)))
}
C_m <- consensus_scores(S_m); all_sc <- cbind(S_m, C_m)
cons_tab <- t(sapply(all_sc, function(s) c(AUC = roc_auc(y_m, s),
                                           BEDROC20 = rie_bedroc(y_m, s, 20)[2],
                                           EF20 = ef(y_m, s, 0.20))))
knitr::kable(cons_tab, digits = 3)
AUC BEDROC20.BEDROC EF20
max_tanimoto 0.993 0.997 4.894
knn5 0.991 0.995 4.838
qsar_rf 0.968 0.950 4.461
desc_dist 0.867 0.776 3.382
cons_z 0.988 0.994 4.844
cons_rank 0.987 0.984 4.719
cons_vote 0.792 0.985 5.001
cons_ecr 0.988 0.977 4.813 
paired_bootstrap_delta <- function(y, s1, s2, stat = roc_auc, n_boot = 400, seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed); ai <- which(y == 1); di <- which(y == 0); d <- numeric(n_boot)
  for (b in seq_len(n_boot)) {                   # the SAME replicate scores both rankings
    idx <- c(sample(ai, length(ai), TRUE), sample(di, length(di), TRUE))
    d[b] <- stat(y[idx], s1[idx]) - stat(y[idx], s2[idx])
  }
  c(mean(d), unname(quantile(d, 0.025)), unname(quantile(d, 0.975)), mean(d <= 0))
}
cat("paired bootstrap, delta AUC against the best single ranking (max_tanimoto):\n")
## paired bootstrap, delta AUC against the best single ranking (max_tanimoto):
for (c_ in names(C_m)) {
  r <- paired_bootstrap_delta(y_m, C_m[[c_]], S_m$max_tanimoto)
  cat(sprintf("  %-10s %+.4f [%+.4f, %+.4f]  P(delta <= 0) = %.3f\n", c_, r[1], r[2], r[3], r[4]))
}
##   cons_z     -0.0051 [-0.0100, -0.0010]  P(delta <= 0) = 0.990
##   cons_rank  -0.0065 [-0.0097, -0.0035]  P(delta <= 0) = 1.000
##   cons_vote  -0.2016 [-0.2178, -0.1858]  P(delta <= 0) = 1.000
##   cons_ecr   -0.0049 [-0.0078, -0.0022]  P(delta <= 0) = 1.000
pair <- rowMeans(scale(as.matrix(S_m[, c("qsar_rf", "desc_dist")])))
r <- paired_bootstrap_delta(y_m, pair, S_m$qsar_rf)
cat(sprintf("\nz-consensus of the two WEAK rankings vs the better of them: AUC %.3f vs %.3f, delta %+.4f [%+.4f, %+.4f]\n",
            roc_auc(y_m, pair), roc_auc(y_m, S_m$qsar_rf), r[1], r[2], r[3]))
## 
## z-consensus of the two WEAK rankings vs the better of them: AUC 0.955 vs 0.968, delta -0.0129 [-0.0187, -0.0078]
ct <- data.table(ranking = rownames(cons_tab), AUC = cons_tab[, "AUC"])
ct[, kind := ifelse(grepl("^cons", ranking), "consensus", "single")]
ct[, ranking := factor(ranking, levels = ranking[order(AUC)])]
pc1 <- ggplot(ct, aes(AUC, ranking, fill = kind)) + geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0.5, 1)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(single = PAL[["blue"]], consensus = PAL[["orange"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Single rankings vs consensus", y = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")
sp_m <- cor(S_m, method = "spearman")
spdf <- as.data.table(as.table(sp_m)); setnames(spdf, c("a", "b", "rho"))
pc2 <- ggplot(spdf, aes(a, b, fill = rho)) + geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", rho)), size = 2.6, colour = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = PAL[["purple"]], high = PAL[["green"]], limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Spearman correlation between rankings", x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 40, hjust = 1), legend.position = "bottom")
print(pc1 | pc2)

Figure 13. Left: no consensus scheme beats the best single ranking on this panel. The z-score consensus loses 0.005 of AUC, rank-by-rank 0.006, ECR 0.005 and rank-by-vote 0.202; in every case the paired bootstrap interval of the difference excludes zero, so these are small but real losses, not noise. Right: the reason. The two similarity rankings correlate at Spearman 0.97 — they contribute the same information twice — while the two property rankings correlate with them at only 0.48-0.52 and are much weaker, so averaging dilutes the good signal with the bad. Even the consensus of the two weak, comparatively decorrelated rankings fails to beat the better of the pair (0.955 against 0.968, a loss of 0.013 with interval [-0.019, -0.008]).

One nuance worth noting: rank-by-vote is catastrophic on ROC-AUC (0.792) and yet has the highest EF at 20 % of the whole table (5.00). It is a coarse score with only five distinct values, so almost the entire list is tied; the area under the curve punishes those ties heavily, while a metric that only looks at the top 20 % is happy with them. Metric and score granularity interact, which is one more reason to report several metrics.

Consensus is a variance-reduction device, not a free improvement: it pays when components are of similar quality with different failure modes — typically several docking functions on the same poses — and costs when one component is clearly better, which is when the temptation to combine everything is strongest. A paired bootstrap of the metric difference, not two separately reported numbers, is the minimum evidence a consensus claim needs[4].

14. Score-size correlation and ligand efficiency

Screening scores are often correlated with molecular size: bigger molecules make more contacts, so additive scoring functions reward them, and the top of a docking list fills with heavy, greasy compounds that are poor starting points for medicinal chemistry[29]. The remedy is a size-normalised score — ligand efficiency, the free energy of binding per heavy atom, \(\mathrm{LE} = 1.37 \times \mathrm{pActivity} / N_{\text{heavy}}\) in kcal mol-1 per atom[8]. The diagnostic comes first: measure the correlation before correcting for it.

ha <- lib$HeavyAtoms[ev_m]
cat("Spearman correlation of each score with heavy-atom count:\n")
## Spearman correlation of each score with heavy-atom count:
for (c_ in names(S_m))
  cat(sprintf("   %-13s rho = %+.3f\n", c_, cor(S_m[[c_]], ha, method = "spearman")))
##    max_tanimoto  rho = -0.004
##    knn5          rho = +0.016
##    qsar_rf       rho = -0.138
##    desc_dist     rho = -0.159
cat(sprintf("\nranking the library by heavy-atom count ALONE: AUC %.3f (matched decoys), %.3f (random decoys)\n",
            roc_auc(y_m, ha), roc_auc(y_r, lib$HeavyAtoms[ev_r])))
## 
## ranking the library by heavy-atom count ALONE: AUC 0.441 (matched decoys), 0.455 (random decoys)
pact <- lib$pActivity[ev_m][y_m == 1]; ha_a <- ha[y_m == 1]
LE <- 1.37 * pact / ha_a
cat(sprintf("actives: pActivity vs heavy atoms rho = %+.3f | ligand efficiency mean %.3f, sd %.3f kcal/mol per atom, %.0f %% below 0.3\n",
            cor(pact, ha_a, method = "spearman"), mean(LE), sd(LE), 100 * mean(LE < 0.3)))
## actives: pActivity vs heavy atoms rho = +0.043 | ligand efficiency mean 0.377, sd 0.070 kcal/mol per atom, 14 % below 0.3
norm <- S_m$max_tanimoto / ha * 30
cat(sprintf("size-normalising the best score: AUC %.3f (unnormalised %.3f)\n",
            roc_auc(y_m, norm), roc_auc(y_m, S_m$max_tanimoto)))
## size-normalising the best score: AUC 0.987 (unnormalised 0.993)
sz <- data.table(ha = ha, s = S_m$max_tanimoto, y = factor(y_m, labels = c("decoys", "actives")))
pl1 <- ggplot(sz, aes(ha, s, colour = y)) + geom_point(size = 0.4, alpha = 0.25) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(decoys = PAL[["blue"]], actives = PAL[["orange"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Similarity score vs size (rho = 0.00)", x = "heavy atoms", y = "max Tanimoto") +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.8, 0.8), legend.text = element_text(size = 6))
pl2 <- ggplot(data.table(ha = ha_a, p = pact), aes(ha, p)) +
  geom_point(size = 0.5, alpha = 0.3, colour = PAL[["orange"]]) +
  labs(title = "Potency vs size (actives)", x = "heavy atoms", y = "pActivity")
pl3 <- ggplot(data.table(LE = LE), aes(LE)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = PAL[["green"]]) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.3, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = 0.305, y = 60, label = "0.3: usual lead criterion", hjust = 0, size = 2.4) +
  labs(title = "Ligand efficiency of the ROCK1 actives",
       x = "ligand efficiency (kcal/mol per heavy atom)", y = "compounds")
print(pl1 | pl2 | pl3)

Figure 14. Left: the maximum-Tanimoto score is uncorrelated with molecular size (Spearman -0.004), and ranking the library by heavy-atom count alone gives AUC 0.441 — below chance, because the actives are slightly smaller than the matched decoys, so the benchmark has no size bias of the usual sign to correct. Centre: among the actives, potency barely rises with size (rho = +0.043). Right: ligand efficiencies average 0.377 kcal mol-1 per heavy atom with a tail below the 0.3 value usually required of a lead (14 % of the actives).

A deliberately negative result, and a useful one: size bias belongs to additive, structure-based scoring functions, not to screening in general, and a fingerprint similarity has no reason to grow with atom count. Correcting anyway costs accuracy — dividing by heavy atoms drops the AUC from 0.993 to 0.987 — by injecting a preference for small molecules. Diagnose first, correct only if needed; ligand efficiency belongs to hit triage, where it ranks confirmed actives for chemical tractability[31]. The two property-based scores do show a mild negative size correlation (-0.131 and -0.159), inherited from the same fact: this set of ROCK1 actives is smaller than its matched decoys.

15. Building the list the laboratory will actually buy

The campaign ends with a decision: which fifty compounds. Three criteria compete. Score says take the top fifty. Diversity says that fifty analogues of one scaffold test one hypothesis fifty times, so spread the selection over chemotypes. Tractability says remove compounds with known assay-interference substructures (PAINS filters[33]), implausible properties or impossible chemistry. We implement the first two at a realistic 1 % prevalence and measure the trade-off; the third is a filter whose cost in hits should be measured the same way.

FPe <- FP[ev_m, ]; scaf <- lib$scaffold_smiles[ev_m]; s_best <- S_m$max_tanimoto
select_lists <- function(seed, n_pick = 50, sim_cut = 0.6, pool = 500) {
  set.seed(seed)
  ai <- which(y_m == 1); di <- which(y_m == 0)
  n_a <- round(0.01 * length(di) / 0.99)                  # subsample actives to 1 % prevalence
  idx <- c(sample(ai, n_a), di); yy <- y_m[idx]; ss <- s_best[idx]
  o <- order(-ss, method = "radix"); top <- o[1:n_pick]
  chosen <- o[1]
  for (j in o[2:pool]) {                                   # walk down, keep if dissimilar to all kept
    if (length(chosen) == n_pick) break
    if (max(tani(FPe[idx[j], , drop = FALSE], FPe[idx[chosen], , drop = FALSE])) < sim_cut)
      chosen <- c(chosen, j)
  }
  c(hits_top = sum(yy[top]), hits_div = sum(yy[chosen]),
    scaf_top = length(unique(scaf[idx[top]])), scaf_div = length(unique(scaf[idx[chosen]])),
    n_total = n_a + length(di))
}
res <- as.data.table(t(sapply(0:49, select_lists)))
cat(sprintf("library of %d compounds at 1 %% prevalence; 50 compounds purchased, 50 independent simulations\n",
            res$n_total[1]))
## library of 4196 compounds at 1 % prevalence; 50 compounds purchased, 50 independent simulations
cat(sprintf("top-50 by score      : %.1f +/- %.1f hits, %.1f distinct scaffolds\n",
            mean(res$hits_top), sd(res$hits_top), mean(res$scaf_top)))
## top-50 by score      : 40.5 +/- 1.0 hits, 42.7 distinct scaffolds
cat(sprintf("diverse-50 (T < 0.6) : %.1f +/- %.1f hits, %.1f distinct scaffolds\n",
            mean(res$hits_div), sd(res$hits_div), mean(res$scaf_div)))
## diverse-50 (T < 0.6) : 34.2 +/- 2.2 hits, 46.6 distinct scaffolds
cat(sprintf("random 50            : %.2f hits expected\n", 50 * 0.01))
## random 50            : 0.50 hits expected
hl <- melt(res[, .(`top-50 by score` = hits_top, `diverse-50` = hits_div)],
           measure.vars = c("top-50 by score", "diverse-50"), variable.name = "list", value.name = "hits")
ps1 <- ggplot(hl, aes(hits, fill = list)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, position = "identity", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dotted") +
  annotate("text", x = 1.5, y = 8, label = "random 50", hjust = 0, size = 2.5, angle = 90) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`top-50 by score` = PAL[["blue"]], `diverse-50` = PAL[["orange"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "Hits bought (1 % prevalence)", x = "confirmed actives among the 50 purchased", y = "simulations") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
tl <- rbind(data.table(list = "top-50 by score", hits = res$hits_top, scaf = res$scaf_top),
            data.table(list = "diverse-50",      hits = res$hits_div, scaf = res$scaf_div))
ps2 <- ggplot(tl, aes(hits, scaf, colour = list)) + geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`top-50 by score` = PAL[["blue"]], `diverse-50` = PAL[["orange"]]), name = NULL) +
  labs(title = "The trade-off, one point per simulation",
       x = "hits among the 50 purchased", y = "distinct scaffolds among the 50") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
print(ps1 | ps2)

Figure 15. Fifty simulated purchase rounds on a 4,196-compound library containing 42 actives. The fifty best-scoring compounds return 40.5 ± 1.0 confirmed actives spread over 42.7 scaffolds; a Tanimoto < 0.6 dissimilarity filter applied while walking down the list returns 34.2 ± 2.2 actives over 46.6 scaffolds — about six hits traded for about four chemotypes, both far above the 0.5 hits expected from a random fifty. The two point clouds in the right panel do not overlap: the trade is systematic, not a matter of luck.

Whether the trade is worth making is a project decision. To confirm a series, buy the top of the list; to find a new chemotype — the usual reason for screening — the diversity filter is cheap insurance. Report both numbers, expected hits and expected distinct scaffolds, each with its spread over simulations.

Domain context — what “buying fifty compounds” means

A purchase round in this laboratory means ordering milligram quantities of fifty catalogue compounds from a chemical supplier and running them in a biochemical assay at a single concentration, then measuring a full dose-response curve for whatever responds. The cost is dominated by the assay, not the compounds, and the turnaround is weeks. That is why the analytics above matter: the difference between a ranking with hit rate 40 % and one with 4 % is the difference between one purchase round and ten, and the choice of which fifty to buy is the only place where a data scientist’s work becomes an irreversible, costly commitment.

16. What a prospective campaign commits to

Every number in this document is retrospective: the labels existed before the ranking was built. A prospective campaign commits to a protocol in advance and is judged by the assay. The group’s checklist, which doubles as the summary of this unit, is to state in writing before any compound is ordered: the library and its assumed active fraction; the ranking method with its reference set frozen; the metric and the \(\alpha\) or fraction \(f\) it uses; the number of compounds that will be bought; the diversity and filtering rules; the expected number of hits computed as \(k \times \pi \times \mathrm{EF}\); and what result would count as a failure. Published prospective campaigns at very large scale[9][32] report hit rates of a few per cent from libraries of hundreds of millions of molecules — orders of magnitude better than random, and still a large majority of inactive purchases.

Benchmark numbers remain useful for relative decisions — which ranking to trust, how many references to collect, whether consensus earns its pipeline — but they are not predictions. Doing the prevalence arithmetic of section 12 in front of the collaborators, before the money is spent, is what separates a screening report from a screening advertisement[7].

summary_tab <- data.frame(
  question = c("Does the ranking work?", "How much better than random, early?",
               "Is the difference real?", "Does the decoy set matter?",
               "Is the benchmark honest?", "What will a real campaign get?",
               "Does consensus help?", "Is there a size bias?", "Which 50 to buy?"),
  evidence = c(sprintf("ROC-AUC %.3f (max Tanimoto) vs %.3f (descriptor distance)",
                       roc_auc(y_m, S_m$max_tanimoto), roc_auc(y_m, S_m$desc_dist)),
               sprintf("EF20 %.2f, BEDROC(20) %.3f, hit rate at 50 = %.0f %%",
                       ef(y_m, S_m$max_tanimoto, 0.20), rie_bedroc(y_m, S_m$max_tanimoto, 20)[2],
                       100 * mean(y_m[order(-S_m$max_tanimoto, method = "radix")][1:50])),
               sprintf("stratified bootstrap 95 %% CI [%.3f, %.3f]", ci$auc.lo[1], ci$auc.hi[1]),
               sprintf("AUC gain from matched to random decoys: %+.3f (RF), %+.3f (distance)",
                       decoy_cmp["qsar_rf", "AUC_gain"], decoy_cmp["desc_dist", "AUC_gain"]),
               "properties-only RF: 5-fold AUC 0.978 (matched), 0.999 (random)",
               sprintf("at 0.1 %% prevalence: hit rate in top 100 = %.1f %%, %.1f hits per 50 bought",
                       100 * prev_tab$hit_rate_top100[4], prev_tab$expected_hits_in_50[4]),
               sprintf("best consensus %+.4f AUC vs best single (paired bootstrap)",
