The table collects the nine decisions this unit can answer with numbers; the tenth — whether the compounds bind — only an assay can answer.

17. Summary

A virtual screen delivers an ordering, and the analytics of that ordering are a self-contained data-science problem. This unit built four ligand-based rankings of the same 12,018-molecule library from training information only and measured them from first principles in R. ROC-AUC, implemented as the Mann-Whitney statistic, agrees with pROC to six decimals and places maximum Tanimoto similarity (0.993) and the five-nearest-neighbour score (0.991) above a property-based random forest (0.968) and a descriptor distance (0.867). Enrichment factors at 1 % and 5 % were unusable here because three of the four rankings sit on their ceiling 1/prevalence = 6.212; at 20 % they separate the methods again (4.89, 4.84, 4.44, 3.38). BEDROC and RIE weight the purchasable top at the price of a parameter alpha fixed in advance; at alpha = 20 the four rankings score 0.997, 0.995, 0.950 and 0.776, and by alpha = 160 the first three are indistinguishable at 1.000. Stratified bootstrap intervals are narrow here (0.993 [0.989, 0.997] for the best ranking) and would be several times wider on a typical in-house benchmark with fifty actives instead of 797.

The three honest lessons are larger than any of those numbers. First, the benchmark decides the answer: replacing property-matched decoys by random ones lifts the random forest from 0.968 to 0.997 and the descriptor distance from 0.867 to 0.961 while barely touching the similarity rankings, and the number of known actives used as references moves the same algorithm from 0.835 to 0.993, with draws of five references spanning 0.752 to 0.895. Second, a random forest that sees only twelve bulk properties separates actives from matched decoys at 5-fold AUC 0.978 and from random decoys at 0.999, so this benchmark cannot support any claim about learnt pharmacology — the artificial-enrichment diagnostic must be reported with the results. Third, the 16.1 % active fraction of the evaluation set is a fiction: at a realistic 0.1 % the same ranking still has AUC 0.992 and EF1% = 96, but the hit rate among the top hundred falls to 3.9 %, about two hits per fifty compounds purchased.

Consensus did not rescue anything — all four aggregation schemes lost to the best single ranking with paired-bootstrap intervals excluding zero, because two of the four components were weak and the two strong ones were redundant (Spearman 0.97). Size normalisation was equally unnecessary: the similarity score has no size bias to correct (rho = -0.004, size-only AUC 0.441), and imposing ligand efficiency on it costs 0.006 of AUC. Finally, a diversity filter at Tanimoto 0.6 traded about six hits for about four extra scaffolds in a fifty-compound purchase simulated at 1 % prevalence — the kind of trade that should be decided by the aim of the campaign and reported as two numbers, not one.

Three habits carry over. Report the composition of any benchmark (prevalence, decoy provenance, reference set) next to every metric it produced; use a paired test on the same resamples when comparing rankings; and convert retrospective enrichment into prospective expectation before promising anything to a collaborator. Diversity selection connects to the clustering of Unit 15 (Butina’s leader algorithm[21] solves the same task), and the activity cliff[22] — a tiny structural change abolishing activity — is why no similarity ranking is ever more than a prior.

18. Self-assessment

  1. A colleague reports “ROC-AUC 0.95” for a new ligand-based method. Which three pieces of information do you ask for before believing that it is better than maximum Tanimoto similarity?

The decoy set (provenance and whether it is property-matched), the reference set of known actives (how many, and whether it is the same one the baseline used), and the evaluation protocol (hold-out or cross-validation, and whether the baseline was run on exactly the same evaluation molecules). Section 9 showed a 0.16 AUC swing from the size of the reference set and a 0.14 spread across draws of five references, and section 10 a 0.10 swing from the decoy set.

  1. Why did three of the four rankings produce exactly the same EF at 1 % and 5 % in section 5?

Because the enrichment factor is capped at 1/prevalence, and with 16.1 % actives any ranking whose top 1 % and top 5 % contain only actives attains that cap, 6.212. The metric has no resolution left. Either evaluate at a fraction well above the prevalence, or subsample to a realistic prevalence, or use BEDROC.

  1. What exactly does the parameter alpha of BEDROC control, and how should it be chosen?

It sets the exponential decay of the weight given to an active at relative rank x, exp(-alpha x); about 80 % of the weight lies in the top 4/alpha of the list. Choose it before the analysis from the size of the campaign: if you will test a fraction f of the library, alpha near 4/f weights the region you can afford. Choosing alpha after seeing the curves turns the metric into a selection effect.

  1. A property-only random forest separates your actives from your decoys at AUC 0.98. What does that invalidate, and what does it not?

It invalidates any claim that performance on this benchmark demonstrates target-specific learning, because a model with no structural information achieves the same. It does not invalidate relative comparisons between methods evaluated on the identical decoy set, nor does it mean the ranking will fail prospectively — it means the benchmark cannot tell you whether it will.

  1. Your screen has AUC 0.99 and EF at 1 % equal to 96 on a library with one active per thousand compounds. You will buy 50 compounds from the top 1 %. How many hits do you expect, and what is the probability that any given purchased compound is active?

Hit rate = prevalence x EF = 0.001 x 96 = 0.096, so about 4.8 hits in 50 purchases and a 9.6 % probability per compound. Against a random draw (0.05 hits) that is a factor of 96, and it still means roughly 45 inactive purchases. Note that the simulation in section 12 bought the top 100 of the whole list rather than 50 from the top 1 %, and returned 3.9 %: the arithmetic is only as good as the assumption that the top f is uniform in quality.

  1. Why must the bootstrap used for a screening metric resample actives and decoys separately?

Because EF, BEDROC and hit rate all depend on the prevalence of the evaluation set. Resampling the pooled list lets the number of actives fluctuate, mixing uncertainty about the metric with uncertainty about the benchmark composition, and inflating the interval. Stratified resampling holds the composition fixed, which is the quantity being studied.

  1. Under what conditions does consensus scoring help, and how would you demonstrate that it helped?

When the component rankings are of comparable quality and make uncorrelated errors. Demonstrate it with a paired bootstrap of the metric difference on the same resamples, reporting the interval of the difference; two separately quoted AUCs are not evidence. In this unit all four schemes lost to the best single ranking, with intervals excluding zero.

  1. A docking campaign returns a top list dominated by molecules of 45-55 heavy atoms. What do you check, and what do you do?

Check the Spearman correlation between score and heavy-atom count, and the AUC of ranking by size alone. If both indicate a size effect, re-rank by a size-normalised score (ligand efficiency) or stratify the selection by size bin, and report both lists. Do not apply the normalisation when the diagnostic is negative, as it was for the similarity scores here, because it destroys information.

  1. Why is a diversity-filtered selection usually preferred over the raw top of the list, even though it buys fewer hits?

Because the purpose of most screens is to find a new chemotype, and fifty analogues of a single scaffold test one chemical hypothesis fifty times. The simulation in section 15 quantified the price: about six hits for about four additional scaffolds. Report both numbers and let the project aim decide.

  1. Which parts of a retrospective evaluation does a bootstrap confidence interval NOT cover?

Everything that is a design choice rather than a sample: the decoy set, the reference actives, the fingerprint and similarity measure, the descriptor list, the model’s hyperparameters and the metric’s alpha. Those are quantified by re-running the analysis under alternative choices, as in sections 9 to 11, and their effect here was an order of magnitude larger than the sampling interval.

  1. You are asked to write the prospective commitment for a fifty-compound campaign. List the items it must contain.

Library and assumed active fraction; ranking method with a frozen reference set; metric with its alpha or fraction f; number of compounds to be purchased; diversity and structural-alert filters; the expected number of hits computed as k x prevalence x EF; and the result that would count as a failure. All of it written before the order is placed.

  1. The same method gives AUC 0.81 on your benchmark and 0.92 in the paper that proposed it. Name three mundane explanations before concluding that your implementation is wrong.

A different number or identity of reference actives (Figure 9: 0.75 to 0.90 across draws of five, 0.89 to 0.95 across draws of twenty-five); a different decoy set (Figure 10: up to 0.10 of AUC); and a different evaluation subset or prevalence. Only after those are matched does a discrepancy point at the code.

Glossary

Active
A compound experimentally confirmed to act on the target above a stated potency threshold; here, ROCK1 inhibitors with pActivity at least 6.5.
Decoy
A molecule assumed inactive, added to a benchmark so that a ranking can be scored. Property-matched decoys resemble the actives in bulk properties; random decoys do not.
Prevalence (active fraction)
Proportion of actives in the evaluated set. Determines the ceiling of the enrichment factor and the hit rate of any purchase.
ROC curve / ROC-AUC
True-positive rate against false-positive rate along the ranked list; its area is the probability that a random active outranks a random decoy.
Enrichment factor (EF)
Hit rate in the top fraction f divided by the hit rate of the whole library; bounded above by 1/prevalence.
BEDROC / RIE
Early-recognition metrics that weight an active at relative rank x by exp(-alpha x); BEDROC is RIE rescaled to [0, 1] at the given prevalence.
Hit rate at k
Fraction of actives among the first k compounds of the ranking - the quantity a purchase decision is made on.
Artificial enrichment
Separability of actives from decoys that comes from benchmark construction (property differences) rather than from target pharmacology.
Analogue bias
Over-representation of close analogues among the actives, which inflates similarity-based metrics because one scaffold is found many times.
Tanimoto coefficient
Shared bits divided by the union of set bits of two fingerprints; the standard similarity for Morgan fingerprints, written here as sparse-matrix algebra.
Consensus / rank aggregation
Combining several rankings by averaging standardised scores, averaging ranks, counting votes or summing exponentially weighted ranks (ECR).
Ligand efficiency
1.37 x pActivity divided by the heavy-atom count: potency per atom, used to compare molecules of different size.
Scaffold (Bemis-Murcko)
The ring systems and their linkers after side chains are removed; the usual unit of chemical-series bookkeeping.
Prospective validation
Buying and testing compounds selected by a frozen protocol; the only evaluation immune to benchmark artefacts.
